chapters.title: Chapter 6: Risk, Tax and Getting Started

lessons.title: Getting Started: Opening a Commodity Account and Planning Your First Trade

children.text: You now understand more about commodity markets than most people who trade them: contract specs, margins, MTM, rollovers, the curve, what drives gold, crude and jeera, how things go wrong, and how profits are taxed. This lesson turns that knowledge into a careful first step. By the end of it you will know how to open and activate a commodity trading account in India, what the broker will ask for and why, how money and contract notes flow, how to write a complete trade plan before you place a single order, and how to structure your first month so that your early mistakes are small and cheap.

body.text: Your first commodity trades are tuition, not income. Make them small, planned in writing and reviewed afterwards, so that the lessons are cheap and your capital survives to use them.

children.text: Step 1: Choose a Broker and Open the Account

To trade MCX or NCDEX contracts, you need a trading account with a SEBI-registered stock broker that is a member of the commodity exchange you want. Many large brokers, including Zerodha, Upstox, Angel One, ICICI Direct and Kotak Securities, offer MCX trading alongside equities.

body.caption: What to compare when choosing a broker for commodities

cells: Does the broker offer MCX, NCDEX or both, and the specific contracts you want?
Brokerage per order, plus how clearly exchange charges, CTT, stamp duty and GST are shown
Quality of charts, order types, margin calculator and position screen during the evening session
When the broker squares off positions, how it handles tender and delivery periods, and whether physical delivery is supported
Availability of support during late evening trading hours
SEBI registration number and exchange membership, verifiable on the SEBI and exchange websites

children.text: Step 2: Activate the Commodity Segment

A standard account usually starts with equity cash trading only. Derivatives segments, including commodities, need separate activation, because SEBI rules require brokers to assess whether clients have the financial capacity for leveraged products.
Proof of income.
Brokers typically accept documents such as a recent bank statement, salary slips, Form 16, an ITR acknowledgement, a net worth certificate or a demat holdings statement.
Risk disclosure.
You must read and accept the risk disclosure document for derivatives. Read it; it describes exactly the risks covered in this course.
Segment selection.
Select the commodity derivatives segment in your broker's profile or segment settings, then wait for confirmation.
A commodity demat account is only for delivery.
To hold commodities received through physical delivery, you would need an account with a commodity repository. For cash-settled contracts such as crude oil, you do not need one.

body.title: What do you actually need?
body.question: Harish only wants to trade MCX Crude Oil Mini futures, which are cash settled. Which of these does he NOT need?
options: A trading account with a SEBI-registered broker that is an MCX member
Activation of the commodity derivatives segment
Acceptance of the risk disclosure document
An account with a commodity repository to hold physical commodities
body.explanation: A commodity repository account is needed only to hold commodities received through physical delivery. Cash-settled crude oil contracts never involve delivery, so Harish needs a broker account, segment activation and the signed risk disclosure, but not a commodity repository account.

children.text: Step 3: Understand How Money Moves
Add funds only from your own registered bank account.
Brokers accept transfers through UPI, net banking or NEFT from bank accounts linked to your trading account. Never pay any individual.
Margin is blocked when you trade.
The required margin is blocked from your balance when the order executes.
MTM moves daily.
Gains and losses are credited or debited at the end of each day, as covered in Chapter 2.
Collateral margin has limits.
Pledged shares or funds can provide collateral margin, but exchanges generally require a minimum portion of derivatives margin in cash.
Unused funds come back periodically.
Under SEBI rules, brokers must settle clients' unused funds back to their bank accounts on a regular monthly or quarterly cycle, as the client chooses.

body.label: Your records
body.context: After each trading day, your broker sends a digital contract note listing every trade, price and charge. Exchanges also send trade confirmation messages to your registered mobile and email. Check them; they are your proof if anything is ever disputed.

body.text: Never share your login password, TOTP or OTPs with anyone, and never let a "trading expert", relative or relationship manager trade your account for you. Unauthorised trading is one of the most common sources of large, disputed losses in leveraged segments.

children.text: Step 4: Write a Trade Plan Before Every Trade

markDefs.definition: A written set of decisions made before entering a trade: the reason, instrument, entry, stop-loss, target, position size, holding period and exit rules.

children.text: A
trade plan
forces you to make every important decision while you are calm, before money is at risk. If you cannot fill in every line, you are not ready to trade.

body.caption: A complete trade plan: Crude Oil Mini example (illustrative prices)

cells: OPEC+ is expected to extend supply cuts, and US inventories have fallen for three weeks, so crude may rise over the next one to two weeks
A decisive fall below recent support, or an OPEC+ decision to raise output
MCX Crude Oil Mini futures, next month contract, cash settled against NYMEX WTI
₹5,640, which is ₹240 below entry and about 1.5 times the recent average true range
Risk per lot = ₹240 × 10 barrels = ₹2,400, so 1 lot
EIA inventory report Wednesday 8:00 pm IST; OPEC+ meeting on the weekend
Exit at stop or target; reduce before the OPEC+ weekend if the trade is not in profit; close well before contract expiry

body.title: Reward-to-risk
body.prompt: In the plan above, entry is ₹5,880, the stop is ₹5,640 and the target is ₹6,240. What is the reward-to-risk ratio? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Risk = ₹5,880 minus ₹5,640 = ₹240. Reward = ₹6,240 minus ₹5,880 = ₹360. Ratio = ₹360 ÷ ₹240 = 1.5. From Lesson 1 of this chapter, the breakeven win rate is 1 ÷ (1 + 1.5) = 40%, before costs.

body.title: Why the plan includes "what would prove me wrong"

children.text: Most traders write down why they are right. Very few write down what would make them wrong. That second line is the most valuable one in the plan.
It stops you moving your stop-loss because you "still believe" in the trade.
It separates price noise from a genuine change in the story.
When you review the trade later, it shows whether you lost because the thesis was wrong or because you ignored your own exit.
A stop-loss is where the market proves you wrong on price. The invalidation line is where the facts prove you wrong on the story.
Step 5: Keep a Trading Journal

markDefs.definition: A record of every trade, including the plan, execution, result and a short review of what went right or wrong. It turns experience into measurable improvement.

children.text: A
trading journal
is how you find out whether you actually have an edge, and which mistakes keep costing you.

cells: Nervous before the EIA report; did not change the stop
Pre-planned exit rules made the event easier to handle

children.text: Your First 30 Days

body.title: A careful first month in commodity trading

events.title: Set up
events.description: Open the account, activate the commodity segment, add a small amount of capital you can afford to lose, and explore the platform during the evening session without trading.

events.title: Study the contracts
events.description: Pick one or two contracts. Read their specifications, find their expiry and delivery dates, and mark the key data releases in your calendar.

events.title: Paper trade
events.description: Write full trade plans and track them in your journal without real money. Aim for at least 10 plans so you see how your ideas perform.

events.title: First live trades
events.description: Place your first real trades using the smallest contract that fits your plan, with strict risk per trade.

events.title: Review
events.description: Go through the journal. Did you follow your plans? What did costs, slippage and emotions do to results? Decide whether to continue, adjust or stop.

body.title: Paper trading vs small live trading

columns.label: Paper trading
points: No money at risk, so mistakes are free
Good for learning platforms, contract maths and planning
Does not capture fear, greed or slippage

columns.label: Small live trading
points: Real but limited money at risk
Reveals how you behave under pressure
Includes real costs, slippage and execution
The only way to learn whether you can follow your own rules

body.text: Smaller contracts make learning cheaper. Gold Petal covers just 1 gram, Silver Micro covers 1 kg and Crude Oil Mini covers 10 barrels. Starting there means the same mistakes cost a fraction of what they would on full-size contracts.

children.text: When Something Goes Wrong
If you have a problem with your broker, such as an unauthorised trade, a wrong debit or an unfair square-off, follow the escalation path.
Raise it with the broker in writing.
Use the broker's grievance email or support ticket, and keep records.
Escalate to the exchange.
If unresolved, file a complaint with the exchange's investor services cell.
Use SEBI SCORES.
SEBI's online complaints system tracks complaints against registered intermediaries.
Online dispute resolution.
SEBI's SMART ODR platform offers conciliation and, if needed, online arbitration for disputes with market intermediaries.

body.title: Where to escalate
body.textWithBlank: SEBI's online system for investors to file and track complaints against registered intermediaries is called ___.
body.explanation: SCORES is SEBI's complaints redress system. Start with the broker, then the exchange, and use SCORES and the SMART ODR platform if the issue is not resolved.

body.title: The "sure-shot" call
body.scenario: Neeraj, a 26-year-old in Indore, has just activated his commodity segment. A Telegram channel with 2 lakh followers posts: "SURE-SHOT CRUDE CALL: Buy CRUDEOIL above ₹5,900, target ₹6,300, SL ₹5,850. 95% accuracy. VIP members made ₹4 lakh last week. Join VIP for ₹9,999." Neeraj is tempted to buy 2 full Crude Oil lots on his first day.
body.prompt: What should Neeraj make of this, and what would a sensible first trade look like instead?
body.modelAnswer:
Red flags:
1. "Sure-shot" and "95% accuracy" are claims no legitimate adviser can make about leveraged trades. Past results posted by the channel cannot be verified.
2. Unregistered advice. Giving specific buy and sell recommendations for a fee requires SEBI registration as an investment adviser or research analyst. He should search the name on SEBI's website. SEBI has also barred registered intermediaries from associating with unregistered finfluencers who give advice or make return claims.
3. The stop is unrealistically tight. A ₹50 stop on crude is easily hit by normal noise, which is how "95% accuracy" channels generate losses for followers.
4. Size. Two full Crude Oil lots cover 200 barrels, so every ₹100 move is ₹20,000. On day one, with no experience, that is far too large.

A sensible first trade: his own written plan, based on a reason he understands, in Crude Oil Mini or another small contract, with a stop set by volatility, position size from 1% risk per trade, awareness of the events during the holding period, and a journal entry to review afterwards.

body.title: Ready for your first live commodity trade?
steps: My account is with a SEBI-registered broker that is a member of the right exchange, and the commodity segment is active.
I have read the contract specification, expiry date and settlement type for my chosen contract.
I have a written trade plan with thesis, invalidation, entry, stop, target, size and exit rules.
My risk on this trade is within my personal limit, and I am using the smallest suitable contract.
I know the major data releases and events during my holding period.
I have set up a journal and will review this trade afterwards, win or lose.

body.label: SEBI SCORES
body.description: SEBI's online platform to lodge and track complaints against brokers and other registered market intermediaries.

cards.definition: Enabling commodity derivatives on your trading account, usually with proof of income and a risk disclosure.
The document explaining the risks of derivatives trading that clients must accept before trading.
Needed only to hold commodities received through physical delivery.
The broker's daily record of your trades, prices and charges.
Periodic return of unused client funds to the bank account, monthly or quarterly.
Written decisions on thesis, invalidation, entry, stop, target, size and exit before trading.
A record of plans, results and reviews for every trade.
SEBI's complaint system and online dispute resolution platform.

points: Open an account with a SEBI-registered broker that is a member of MCX or NCDEX, and compare charges, platform, risk policies and support.
Activate the commodity segment with proof of income and the risk disclosure; a commodity repository account is needed only for physical delivery.
Move money only from your own bank account, check contract notes, and never share login credentials or let anyone trade for you.
Write a full trade plan before every trade, including what would prove you wrong, and size it from your risk budget.
Keep a journal, paper trade first, then start live with the smallest suitable contracts.
If something goes wrong, escalate from broker to exchange to SEBI SCORES and SMART ODR.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation of any broker or trade. Broker names are examples, not endorsements. Account opening requirements and regulations change; check current requirements with your broker and SEBI. The trade plan uses illustrative prices. Commodity derivatives are leveraged and can cause losses larger than your initial margin.
